# Optimization and Parallelization

Also called: Distributed 3DGS Training, Per-Splat Backpropagation, Mask Gradient Computation

## Overview
This family encompasses algorithmic strategies to accelerate the training of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and extend its scalability to scenes exceeding single-GPU memory limits. It addresses the computational bottleneck of the differentiable rasterization backward pass and the memory constraints of large-scale scene reconstruction. It is distinguished from standard optimization by replacing the per-pixel gradient accumulation with per-splat accumulation to avoid atomic contention [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation], partitioning Gaussian primitives across multiple GPUs for distributed training [7349-grendel-gs], and explicitly computing gradients for probabilistic masks during alpha blending [4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation].

## Shared principles
The methods in this family share the following foundational mechanisms:

1.  **Differentiable Rasterization Core**: All methods rely on the differentiable alpha-blending rasterizer. The forward pass computes pixel color $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x})$ via depth-sorted alpha blending, and the backward pass computes gradients $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta}$ with respect to Gaussian parameters $\theta$ [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].
2.  **Gradient Accumulation**: Gradients are accumulated over multiple training steps or views before an optimizer update. In distributed settings, gradients or intermediate rendering states are synchronized across devices [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].
3.  **Adaptive Representation**: Many optimization variants modify the Gaussian representation or its distribution to improve efficiency or fidelity, requiring corresponding adjustments to the gradient computation or data flow [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].
4.  **Hardware Acceleration**: Methods leverage GPU parallelism, often using CUDA kernels, Tensor Cores (via GEMM reformulation), or half-precision arithmetic to accelerate the rasterization and gradient computation [6233-optimization-and-parallelization].

## Subtopics

### [MaskGaussian Gradient Computation](4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation.md)
A method for computing the gradient of the loss with respect to probabilistic masks $\mathcal{M}_i$ applied to 3D Gaussians. It distinguishes itself by explicitly accounting for the gradient contribution of the mask on both the foreground Gaussian color accumulation and the background transmittance path, solving the problem of backpropagating through masked alpha-blending. Choose this when training requires learnable masks to modulate Gaussian opacity.

### [Training Pipeline](5325-training-pipeline.md)
The iterative optimization loop that initializes Gaussians and optimizes their parameters via gradient descent. It distinguishes itself by integrating dynamic Gaussian management (pruning, densification, cloning) within the training loop to adapt representation density to scene complexity. Choose this as the standard baseline for 3DGS reconstruction.

### [Parallelization for Backpropagation](5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation.md)
A training optimization that replaces the standard per-pixel backward pass with a per-splat (per-Gaussian) approach. It distinguishes itself by iterating over Gaussians and updating the gradients of the pixels they cover, addressing the performance bottleneck of atomic contention in the per-pixel approach. Choose this to reduce training time by 4–5× while maintaining numerical equivalence.

### [Grendel-GS](7349-grendel-gs.md)
A distributed optimization framework that partitions the Gaussian primitive list across multiple GPUs. It distinguishes itself from single-machine streaming methods by distributing the parameter table across a GPU cluster, enabling training on scenes with billions of primitives. Choose this when scene size exceeds single-GPU VRAM capacity.

### [3D Gaussian Splatting Implementation Details](9128-3d-gaussian-splatting-implementation-details.md)
Details the specific algorithmic steps, hyperparameters, and data structures for stable implementation. It distinguishes itself by providing concrete values for optimization schedules, densification thresholds, and memory management strategies (such as half-precision rasterization). Choose this for reference implementation values and stability guards.

## Background
3D Gaussian Splatting was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 [6233-optimization-and-parallelization]. The initial implementation used a per-pixel backward pass which suffered from atomic contention. Subsequent works identified bottlenecks in memory bandwidth and scalability, leading to per-splat backpropagation [5989-parallelization-for-backpropagation] and distributed frameworks like Grendel-GS [7349-grendel-gs]. Mask-based gradient computation [4254-maskgaussian-gradient-computation] addresses specific variants involving probabilistic masking. Implementation details such as half-precision training [9128-3d-gaussian-splatting-implementation-details] and adaptive densification [5325-training-pipeline] have become standard practices to ensure convergence and efficiency.
